tldr: The authors propose STAR, an integrated training recipe that overcomes the severe spatial, temporal, and informational sparsity of tactile signals in multi-finger hands, along with a 200-hour real-world dexterous manipulation dataset, achieving diverse contact-rich tasks with just 100 post-training demonstrations.
hero_caption: Overall view of the STAR integrated training recipe. It is built on three pillars: a) visual-tactile joint pre-training that simultaneously reconstructs masked visual and tactile images, b) sparse-global tactile token representations combining activated contact tokens with per-hand global tokens, and c) an auxiliary task predicting sparse future tactile signals distributed across the action horizon.
overview:
Achieving human-like dexterous manipulation with multi-finger robotic hands has long been a dream in robotics, but two major obstacles have stood in the way: a critical shortage of high-quality real-world data involving coordinated multi-finger control, and the extreme sparsity of tactile signals from multi-finger hands, making representation learning difficult. Although tactile sensors are distributed across the entire hand, only a tiny fraction of sensing elements make contact with objects (spatial sparsity), no signals appear during reaching phases (temporal sparsity), and tactile sensing alone captures only localized contact without broader context (informational sparsity)—a challenging triple sparsity.

To address this, the authors built a high-precision data collection platform from scratch and gathered a high-quality real-world bimanual dataset of over 10,000 trajectories across 200 hours, with dexterous multi-finger manipulation making up about 70% of the data. On top of this, they propose STAR, a training recipe designed to tackle tactile sparsity directly. STAR prevents overfitting to empty signals through visual-tactile joint pre-training, removes redundancy via a sparse-global tactile token representation that retains only contact tokens and a per-hand summary token, and captures contact dynamics by predicting future tactile states distributed across the entire action horizon.

When evaluated on four challenging real-world tasks with a bimanual dexterous robot—such as earbud flipping and stacked-book retrieval—STAR achieved an average success rate of 61% with only 100 post-training trajectories per task. It significantly outperformed existing leading VLA models (like GR00T and LDA-1B), and ablations proved that each of the three components is essential.
contributions: Built a real-world system equipped with 10-DoF hands and 268-dimensional tactile sensing, collecting a large-scale bimanual dataset of 200 hours and 10,576 trajectories, with 69.5% involving dexterous multi-finger manipulation.

Proposed STAR, an integrated recipe addressing spatial, temporal, and informational sparsity in dexterous tactile signals through visual-tactile joint pre-training, sparse-global tactile token representations, and sparse future tactile prediction.

Achieved an average success rate of 61% across four challenging real-world manipulation tasks with only 100 post-training trajectories per task, substantially outperforming existing foundation models.

sections.heading: The Triple Sparsity Hurdle in Multi-Finger Hands
sections.summary: Dexterous multi-finger manipulation requires tactile feedback, but the lack of real-world data and the extreme sparsity of tactile signals make learning challenging. To tackle this, the paper introduces a 200-hour high-quality dataset and STAR, an integrated training recipe designed to overcome this sparsity.
sections.details:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-finger robotic hands has long been an aspiration in robotics research. However, conventional robot learning models have often been limited to simple pick-and-place tasks using two-finger parallel grippers. Stepping up to sophisticated multi-finger manipulation demands both large-scale real-world data and learning methods that effectively utilize tactile signals.

Yet, learning from multi-finger tactile data presents unique difficulties due to the "triple sparsity" of tactile signals:
- Spatial sparsity: Out of many sensor elements (taxels, the tactile equivalent of pixels), only a tiny fraction are ever in contact with an object.
- Temporal sparsity: Tactile signals remain zero for most of an execution trajectory, such as when the hand is reaching toward an object.
- Informational sparsity: Tactile feedback reflects only hyper-local contact states and lacks the global context provided by vision.

Existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) rely on massive datasets to learn with weak inductive biases, but collecting multi-finger tactile data at web-scale is impossible. Therefore, the authors designed STAR, an integrated recipe embedded with strong inductive biases. By combining visual-tactile joint pre-training, sparse-global token representations, and sparse future tactile prediction, the model achieves a 61% real-world success rate with only 100 post-training demonstrations per task.

sections.heading: Where Did Prior Methods Fall Short?
sections.summary: While human videos and simulation data scale easily, they suffer from large embodiment and dynamics gaps, making them unsuitable for contact-rich tasks. Furthermore, existing tactile models are designed for two-finger grippers and cannot handle the severe spatial sparsity of multi-finger hands.
sections.details:
### II-A Current Landscape of Multi-Finger Data Sources
Data for multi-finger hands generally falls into "out-of-robot data" and "in-robot data." Human videos and wearable capture setups scale well, but kinematic and skeletal mismatches (the embodiment gap) and the absence of force information cap their performance on contact-rich tasks. Conversely, simulated data struggles with sim-to-real gaps, especially regarding complex contact mechanics and sensor noise. Ultimately, high-quality real-world teleoperation data is most desirable, but the low durability of hands and tactile sensors, along with the difficulty of teleoperation, has kept prior datasets biased toward simple skills.

### II-B Foundation Models for Dexterous Manipulation
Recent efforts attempt to pre-train policies using mixed data from human videos and two-finger grippers to achieve generalist manipulation. However, these methods suffer from severe distribution shifts when applied to contact-rich multi-finger tasks. As a result, success rates plummet on anything beyond simple pick-and-place actions.

### II-C Challenges in Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) Models
Prior VTLA models primarily targeted two-finger parallel grippers with only two sensor pads. For grippers, simple gating mechanisms that inject tactile tokens only when contact occurs were sufficient to handle temporal sparsity. In contrast, multi-finger hands feature hundreds of taxels packed across the palm and fingers. Naively tokenizing all of them floods the model with useless non-contact tokens. Prior work only addressed narrow aspects of this sparsity and lacked a unified framework spanning pre-training to policy learning.

sections.heading: Formulating Action Generation via Conditional Flow Matching
sections.summary: The authors frame manipulation as predicting future joint and end-effector trajectories (action chunks) conditioned on multi-camera images, bimanual tactile feedback, robot proprioception, and language instructions, using Conditional Flow Matching for generation.
sections.details:
This work models the conditional probability distribution $p(a_t | o_t)$ of an upcoming action chunk $a_t = \{a_t^1, \dots, a_t^H\}$ given an observation $o_t = \{I_t, T_t, s_t, l_t\}$.
The variables are defined as follows:
- $I_t$: Multi-camera visual inputs (left and right wrist cameras, plus a head camera)
- $T_t$: Tactile signals from both hands
- $s_t$: Robot proprioception (arm end-effector pose and hand joint angles)
- $l_t$: Natural language task instruction
- $a_t$: Future arm target poses and hand joint targets for $H$ steps, parameterized relative to the current state $s_t$

For action generation, the authors adopt Conditional Flow Matching (CFM), which trains faster and more stably than Diffusion Policy. Starting from noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, CFM transforms samples toward the target action distribution along a learned velocity field $\mathbf{v}_\theta(a_t^\tau, o_t, \tau)$. During inference, it uses an Euler solver with only 10 integration steps while reusing the Key-Value cache of observation $o_t$, generating smooth action chunks all at once.

sections.heading: Collecting 200 Hours of Data and the STAR Training Recipe
sections.summary: The authors developed a durable bimanual teleoperation system to collect 200 hours of multi-finger data. To tackle tactile sparsity, they train the VLA model using a three-pronged approach: visual-tactile joint pre-training, sparse-global token representation, and sparse future tactile prediction.
sections.details:
### IV-A Building the Real-World Dexterous Manipulation Dataset
To withstand long hours of data collection, the authors constructed a robot with a wheeled mobile base, dual arms, two 10-DoF hands, and piezoresistive tactile sensors totaling 268 taxels across the palms and inner fingers (Fig. F2). For teleoperation, they used motion-tracking gloves to capture fine finger movements and enhanced the DexPilot retargeting algorithm. By adding fingertip contact alignment and posture constraints—and intentionally disabling auto-closure helper mechanisms—operators gained intuitive micro-control. A C++ multi-process implementation minimized system latency. The resulting dataset contains 200 hours, 65 tasks, and 10,576 trajectories, with 69.5% requiring sophisticated multi-finger coordination.

### IV-B1 Visual-Tactile Joint Pre-Training (VTP)
Performing self-supervised pre-training (like MAE) purely on tactile data causes the model to collapse into the trivial solution of predicting all zeros, since the signals are mostly empty. To avoid this, the authors introduce visual-tactile joint pre-training (based on M2VTP). They pair wrist camera RGB images with tactile images and mask 75% of patches from both modalities, reconstructing them simultaneously. Forcing the model to predict tactile cues consistent with visual context prevents it from being misled by spatial sparsity and teaches meaningful tactile features alongside cross-modal alignment.

### IV-B2 Sparse-Global Tactile Token Representation (SGTTR)
Feeding raw tactile patches into a VLM wastes computational resources and attention capacity on vast amounts of inactive tokens. SGTTR discards non-contact tokens completely by masking patches that fall below an activation threshold (Sparse). To ensure the model does not lose overall hand context from local contacts alone, a single learnable global tactile token is maintained for each hand (Global). This global token receives attention from visual and language tokens, but an asymmetric attention mask prevents it from attending back to other modalities, ensuring it serves strictly as a pure tactile summary.

### IV-B3 Sparse Future Tactile Prediction (SFTP)
Past tactile history alone does not provide the model with a clear picture of how contacts will evolve. Therefore, during policy training, the authors add an auxiliary objective: predicting tactile patches at five future timestamps ($T_S=\{10, 20, 30, 40, 50\}$) evenly spaced across the action horizon ($H=50$ steps, roughly 1.67 seconds). Instead of densely predicting a few immediate frames, spreading predictions sparsely across the future bakes long-term, meaningful contact dynamics directly into the representation.

sections.heading: Real-World Experiments: 61% Success Rate and the Impact of Sparsity Handling
sections.summary: Evaluations across four challenging real-world tasks show STAR significantly outperforming models like GR00T and LDA-1B. Ablation experiments prove that VTP, SGTTR, and SFTP are all crucial for effectively leveraging tactile feedback.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
The evaluation covers four tasks: "Earbud flipping" (rotating an earbud 180° with thumb and index finger), "Stacked-book retrieval" (hooking an index finger into a gap to pull out a book), "Postcard retrieval" (sliding a card to the table edge and placing it in a box), and "Multi-object grasping" (picking up multiple trash items sequentially with different finger combinations) (Fig. F5). All tasks are exceedingly difficult for two-finger grippers, and testing was conducted on unseen objects excluded from pre-training. Post-training used 100 demonstrations per task, evaluated across 20 trials each.

### V-B Comparison with Existing Policies
The results demonstrated clear superiority (Table I):
- Ours: Achieved an average Success Rate (SR) of 61.0% and a Task Completion Rate (TCR) of 72.3% across the four tasks.
- GR00T N1.7: Fine-tuning from official weights caused violent arm oscillations triggering safety stops (0% SR). Even when pre-trained on the authors' dexterous data, SR peaked at only 15.0%.
- LDA-1B: Pre-trained on human videos, but its latent representations are too high-level for micro-positioning, yielding 8.8% SR (27.5% even after adding dexterous data).
- $\pi_{0.5}$: While possessing accurate arm trajectories from massive two-finger gripper data, it lacks native support for multi-finger hands and touch, reaching only 37.5% SR.

### V-C Ablation: What Drives the Performance?
Ablations stripping down STAR's components revealed key insights (Table II):
- Without VTP (Joint Pre-training): SR dropped sharply to 48.8%. Lacking initial vision-tactile alignment, the policy cannot utilize tactile inputs effectively.
- Without STTR (Sparse Token Selection): SR fell to 51.3%. Non-contact tokens degraded performance, particularly on geometric tasks like book retrieval.
- Without GTTR (Global Tokens): SR decreased to 50.0%. Performance degraded heavily on earbud flipping, which requires frequent fingertip contacts, highlighting the need for a global summary of hand contact states.
- Prediction Horizon Comparison (SFTP vs. DFTP): Concentrating the 5 predicted frames within the immediate 0.17 seconds (DFTP) yielded only 48.8% SR. Sparsely spacing them across the full 1.67-second horizon (SFTP, 55.0% SR) was far superior for learning contact dynamics.

### V-D The Role and Limitations of Tactile Sensing
Completely removing tactile input (Ours w/o T) resulted in a 50.0% SR. Tactile feedback was most impactful in earbud flipping, where fingertip sensing jumped the success rate from 45% to 65%. Conversely, the current robot hands lack sensor elements on the "sides" of the fingers (Fig. F6). In tasks like multi-object grasping where items were pinched using the side of the little finger, the sensor could not detect contact; the model over-relied on tactile input and ignored visual cues, exposing an intriguing hardware-software mismatch.

sections.heading: Current Limitations: Sensor Blind Spots and Language Alignment
sections.summary: Task diversity and dataset size remain modest compared to parallel-gripper data, and blind spots exist on the finger sides. Future work must also address direct tactile-language alignment and generalization across different hardware.
sections.details:
The authors highlight several clear limitations in the paper:
- Data Scale and Diversity: While 200 hours across 65 tasks is substantial for multi-finger manipulation, it remains modest compared to multi-thousand-hour open datasets available for two-finger grippers.
- Sensor Coverage: The hands feature sensors only on the pads and palm, leaving blind spots on the sides and backs of fingers. When contacts occurred in uninstrumented areas, the policy's tendency to rely on touch caused it to neglect vision, leading to failures.
- Language Alignment: While STAR aligns vision and touch, direct alignment between language instructions and tactile signals (e.g., nuances like "press firmly" or "touch gently") is not yet incorporated into pre-training.
- Sensor Noise and Portability: Addressing sensor drift, unit-to-unit variance, wear and tear in piezoresistive arrays, and adapting the method to optical tactile sensors like GelSight remain critical topics for future study.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A New Benchmark for Multi-Finger Tactile Robotics
sections.summary: This work introduces a high-quality 200-hour multi-finger dataset alongside STAR, a recipe that systematically resolves tactile sparsity. The high success rates achieved with minimal fine-tuning prove that foundation models can handle dexterous manipulation when paired with appropriate inductive biases.
sections.details:
This paper offers a practical, systematic solution to the dual roadblocks of dexterous manipulation: data scarcity and the difficulty of processing tactile signals. The 200-hour synchronized dataset (vision, touch, language, and action) forms an invaluable foundation for future dexterous manipulation research.

Methodologically, rather than dumping raw tactile tokens into a VLM, STAR models the intrinsic spatial, temporal, and informational sparsity of touch through joint pre-training (VTP), sparse-global representations (SGTTR), and auxiliary future prediction (SFTP). Achieving a 61% success rate with only 100 trajectories per task proves that with thoughtful architectural choices and proper inductive biases, the foundation model paradigm can successfully unlock dexterous multi-finger manipulation.

takeaways: When feeding multi-finger tactile data to a VLM, filtering out inactive patches and keeping only contact tokens plus a per-hand global summary token (SGTTR) dramatically cuts redundancy.
Self-supervised pre-training (like tactile MAE) on tactile signals alone overfits to predicting all zeros; coupling touch with visual images for cross-modal reconstruction (VTP) is highly effective.
For auxiliary future tactile prediction, distributing targets sparsely across the entire action horizon (SFTP) captures contact dynamics far better than predicting immediate frames densely.

Tactile blind spots (e.g., sides of fingers) can cause the policy to fail if it over-relies on touch at the expense of vision, highlighting the critical balance between sensor placement and multimodal fusion.
limitations: The absence of tactile sensors on the sides of the fingers prevents touch feedback during lateral pinches, sometimes causing failures because the policy underutilizes vision while expecting tactile signals.
Although 200 hours across 65 tasks is large for multi-finger systems, the data scale and task variety are still insufficient to build a truly universal manipulation foundation model.

While visual-tactile alignment is established during pre-training, direct grounding between natural language instructions and tactile forces (such as modulating applied pressure) is not yet supported.
